components.note: 心 (heart) — mind and feelings, as in 想, 思, 感: 总 is simplified from 總, whose threads gathered everything together.
日 (sun) — on top; the usual explanation is sun over 正 "straight, correct": what is clear and straight is "right, is". A memory aid, not firm etymology.

example.pinyin: Tā zǒngshì hěn máng.
example.english: She is always busy.
example.fact: 总是 marks a stable, repeated habit ('she's always busy') — for one unbroken, continuous state rather than a repeated pattern, Chinese instead reaches for 一直 ('continuously, all along'), a habitual-vs-continuous split that English 'always' flattens into one word.

examples.pinyin: Tā zǒngshì chídào.
examples.english: He's always late.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ wèishénme zǒngshì bù shuōhuà?
examples.english: Why are you always so quiet?

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 口 is a mouth, as in 吃, 叫; 嘴 is a mouth or lips.
觜 (zuǐ) — same sound — 嘴 is zuǐ, like 觜.

example.pinyin: Tā de zuǐ hěn tián.
example.english: He has a sweet tongue.
example.fact: 嘴 is the colloquial word for the mouth (as a body part for speaking and eating), whereas 口 is more formal or used in compounds like 人口 and 出口. Idioms like 嘴甜 (sweet-talking) and 多嘴 (to speak out of turn) use it for the way someone talks.

examples.pinyin: Bǎobao zhāngkāi xiǎo zuǐ xiào le.
examples.english: The baby opened her little mouth and laughed.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuǐ lǐ yǒu dōngxi, bié shuōhuà.
examples.english: You have food in your mouth, don't talk.

components.note: ⻊ (foot, form of 足) — feet and walking: 跑 run, 踢 kick, 路 road, 跟 follow; 跳 is a jump.
兆 (zhào) is a loose hint; the series 桃 táo, 逃 táo, 挑 tiāo, 眺 tiào shares the -ao sound.

example.pinyin: Háizimen zài cǎodì shang tiào.
example.english: The children are jumping on the grass.
example.fact: 跳 is used for many bouncing or sudden movements: 跳舞 (dance), 跳高 (high jump), and 心跳 (heartbeat, literally 'heart jump'). It can also describe skipping a step, as in 跳过 ('skip over').

examples.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zài jiā tiàoshéng.
examples.english: She likes skipping rope at home.

examples.hanzi: 小猫从桌子上跳下来了。
examples.pinyin: Xiǎomāo cóng zhuōzi shang tiào xiàlái le.
examples.english: The kitten jumped down from the table.

meanings: to request sb to do sth

components.note: 手 (hand) — two hands joined in respect: bowing and saluting; compare 扌 in 拿 and 打.
扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 打, 拿, 抱: 托 is to hold up with the hand.
乇 (tuō) gives the exact sound.

example.pinyin: Bàituō, bāng wǒ yí gè máng!
example.english: Please, do me a favor!
example.fact: 拜托 literally combines 拜 ('to bow,' pictured as two hands pressed together in respect) with 托 ('to entrust,' held up on an open palm) — 'to bow and entrust a matter to someone' — and today also works as a stand-alone interjection of pleading, much like English 'please!' or 'come on!'

examples.pinyin: Bàituō nǐ bāng wǒ ná yíxià bāo.
examples.english: Please help me hold my bag for a moment.

examples.pinyin: Bàituō, bié zài shuō le!
examples.english: Come on, stop talking already!

components.note: 女 (woman) — a person kneeling with arms crossed; as a radical it heads many female and family words: 妈, 好, 姐.
儿 (child, legs) — shows a person's legs; in 兒 the top was a child's soft skull. As an ending (这儿) it adds the er sound; 儿 also in 先, 兄, 光.

example.pinyin: Tāmen de nǚ'ér jīnnián wǔ suì.
example.english: Their daughter is five years old this year.
example.fact: 女儿 is built as 女 ('female') plus 儿, the very same suffix that independently means 'child, son' in 儿子 ('son') — making 女儿 transparently 'female child,' a mirror image of how 儿子 uses that same 儿.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ nǚ'ér xǐhuan chànggē.
examples.english: My daughter likes singing.

examples.hanzi: 他的女儿在北京读大学。
examples.pinyin: Tā de nǚ'ér zài Běijīng dú dàxué.
examples.english: His daughter attends university in Beijing.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 打, 拿, 抱: to seize.
爪 (zhǎo, claw) is a close sound clue for zhuā and fits the meaning: grab with claws.

example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhuāzhù le xiǎotōu.
example.english: The police caught the thief.
example.fact: 抓 means to grasp with the hand or to arrest, and it has extended meanings like 抓紧 (to make the most of, hurry up) and 抓住机会 (seize the opportunity). It is more forceful and physical than 拿 (to take, hold).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zhuāzhùle tā de shǒu.
examples.english: I grabbed his hand.

examples.pinyin: Xiǎomāo zhuādàole yì zhī lǎoshǔ.
examples.english: The cat caught a mouse.

components.note: 小 (small) — three small dots, tiny grains. As a radical it appears in 少 few, 尖 sharp.
女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈, 她, 好.
且 (qiě) is a loose sound clue for jiě; 且 also sounds out 祖 zǔ, 租 zū and 助 zhù.

example.pinyin: Nà wèi xiǎojie shì shéi?
example.english: Who is that young lady?
example.fact: 小姐 traditionally addressed any young, usually unmarried woman and still works as the standard polite way to address a waitress or shop assistant in Taiwan and Hong Kong — but in mainland China it has also picked up a slang sense of "sex worker," which is why many mainland speakers now prefer the safer 女士 (also in this batch) instead.

examples.hanzi: 这位小姐想买一条围巾。
examples.pinyin: Zhè wèi xiǎojie xiǎng mǎi yì tiáo wéijīn.
examples.english: This young lady would like to buy a scarf.

examples.pinyin: Wáng xiǎojie zài yínháng shàngbān.
examples.english: Miss Wang works at a bank.

components.note: 力 (strength) — effort and motion, as in 办, 助, 努. The part 云 stands in for 重 in the traditional 動, which was the sound clue.

example.pinyin: Bié dòng, wǒ gěi nǐ pāi zhāng zhào.
example.english: Don't move, I'll take a photo of you.
example.fact: 动 is a verb on its own (别动 'don't move') and a very productive component: 运动 (sport), 动物 (animal), 感动 (to be moved), 动手 (to start doing). It also works as a result complement meaning 'able to move', as in 搬不动 ('can't move it').

examples.pinyin: Zhège wánjù huì dòng.
examples.english: This toy can move.

examples.pinyin: Zhège gùshi ràng wǒ hěn gǎndòng.
examples.english: This story moved me a lot.

components.note: 贝 (cowry shell, money) — wealth and trade: 财, 费, 买, 货; 赢 is to win or gain a profit.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen duì yíng le bǐsài.
example.english: Our team won the match.
example.fact: 赢 is the opposite of 输 (shū, to lose). It takes a thing won or an opponent: 赢了比赛 (won the match) or 赢了他 (beat him), and learners should not confuse it with 胜 (shèng, victory), which is more formal.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ cāi shéi huì yíngdé bǐsài?
examples.english: Guess who will win the match?

examples.pinyin: Tā zài yóuxì lǐ yíngle wǒ.
examples.english: He beat me in the game.

components.note: 氵 (water) — water and flow, as in 河, 海, 清: water draining away.
肖 (xiāo) gives the exact sound; also in 销 xiāo and 削 xuē.
自 (nose) — over 心 heart: breath comes through the nose from the heart, so rest, news.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gāng shōudào yí gè hǎo xiāoxi.
example.english: I just received some good news.
example.fact: 消 alone means "to disappear, dissolve" and 息 means "to rest, breathe" — in classical Chinese 消息 first described the waxing and waning of the seasons or of yin and yang, an old astronomical sense that only later narrowed down to today's everyday meaning, "news."

examples.pinyin: Nǐ kàndào wǒ de xiāoxi le ma?
examples.english: Did you see my message?

examples.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi shì zhēn de ma?
examples.english: Is this news true?

components.note: 女 (woman) — a person kneeling with arms crossed; as a radical it heads many female and family words: 妈, 好, 姐.

example.pinyin: Zhè wèi nǚshì shì wǒ de lǎoshī.
example.english: This lady is my teacher.
example.fact: 女 is mostly a bound form in modern Chinese: you say 女人 (woman) or 女孩 (girl) rather than 女 alone. It is also a very common radical in characters about women and family relationships, such as 妈, 姐 and 好.

examples.pinyin: Tā yǒu yí ge nǚ'ér.
examples.english: She has a daughter.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen bān nǚshēng bǐ nánshēng duō.
examples.english: Our class has more girls than boys.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — feelings, as in 快, 怕, 情: a heart with no rest.
亡 (wáng) is a close sound clue for máng; 亡 also in 忘 wàng, 望 wàng and 盲 máng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān hěn máng.
example.english: I am very busy today.
example.fact: 忙 is an adjective, so it takes 很 rather than a verb 'to be': 我很忙. It also works as a verb, as in 忙着做饭 (busy cooking), and in the reply 'nǐ zài máng shénme?' ('what are you busy with?'), a casual way to ask what someone has been up to.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuìjìn máng bu máng?
examples.english: Have you been busy lately?

examples.pinyin: Tā zhèng mángzhe zuòfàn ne.
examples.english: He's busy cooking.

components.note: 戈 (halberd) — a weapon guarding a place 口: 或 first meant a defended territory (域 yù adds 土). "Perhaps, or" is a later use.
讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 谢: giving permission is spoken.
午 (wǔ) is only a loose sound clue for xǔ.

example.hanzi: 他或许已经知道了这件事。
example.pinyin: Tā huòxǔ yǐjīng zhīdào le zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He may already know about this.
example.fact: 或许 sits at the more formal, written end of the "maybe" spectrum — 可能 and 也许 are the everyday spoken defaults, while 或许 shows up more in writing or careful speech, a register distinction the English gloss "perhaps" does not capture.

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān huòxǔ huì xiàyǔ.
examples.english: It might rain tomorrow.

examples.hanzi: 他或许不想去,你问问他。
examples.pinyin: Tā huòxǔ bù xiǎng qù, nǐ wènwen tā.
examples.english: Maybe he doesn't want to go; ask him.

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family terms, as in 妈 mom, 好 good, 姐 sister; 女 (nǚ) also loosely echoes the rú sound.
口 (mouth) — speech; 如 originally meant "to follow, accord with", later "as, like"; also in 汝 rǔ and 茹 rú.
此 (cǐ) is a sound clue for 紫 zǐ, 雌 cí and 些 xiē; as a word it means "this".

example.pinyin: Qíngkuàng bù yīnggāi rúcǐ zāogāo.
example.english: The situation shouldn't be this bad.
example.fact: 如此 is a formal, somewhat literary stand-in for the everyday 这么/那么 (both from the pilot batch) — it turns up constantly in writing and news broadcasts but sounds a little stiff in casual chat, where 这么 would be the natural choice.

examples.pinyin: Tā wèishénme rúcǐ shēngqì?
examples.english: Why is he so angry?

examples.pinyin: Shìqing jiùshì rúcǐ jiǎndān.
examples.english: It's just that simple.

components.note: 阝 (mound, left-side form of 阜 hill) — hills and places: 院, 阳, 陆; 队 is a group of people gathered together.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen shì yí gè duì.
example.english: We are one team.
example.fact: 队 is used in 排队 (to line up, queue), 足球队 (football team), and 队长 (team captain). In everyday speech it is a collective noun and rarely takes the measure word 个, though 一个队 is acceptable.

examples.pinyin: Tóngxuémen páihǎo duì le.
examples.english: The students lined up.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen duì jīntiān yǒu bǐsài.
examples.english: Our team has a game today.

components.note: 無 (traditional) — began as a person dancing with ornaments (same root as 舞). 'None' is a borrowed sense; 无 is an old variant of 無 and the shape does not explain it.
氵 (water) — water, as in 河, 海, 清: in the old form 灋, water stood for fairness, so law and method.

example.pinyin: Tā wúfǎ jiějué zhège wèntí.
example.english: He is unable to solve this problem.
example.fact: 无法 is always followed directly by a verb (无法解决 "unable to solve", 无法忘记 "unable to forget") and never by a bare noun — a learner reaching for 无法 the way English uses "no way to get a thing" will find the grammar does not work that way.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ wúfǎ huídá zhège wèntí.
examples.english: I'm unable to answer this question.

examples.hanzi: 大雪让火车无法开出去。
examples.pinyin: Dàxuě ràng huǒchē wúfǎ kāi chūqù.
examples.english: The heavy snow made it impossible for the train to leave.

components.note: 户 (door) — doors and houses, as in 所 and 扇: a room with a door.
方 (fāng) is a close sound clue for fáng; 方 also sounds out 放 fàng and 访 fǎng.
子 (child) — a picture of a baby with arms outstretched and legs bundled. As a suffix (孩子, 房子) it is a light noun ending.

example.pinyin: Tāmen mǎi le yí tào xīn fángzi.
example.english: They bought a new house.
example.fact: 房子 takes the measure word 套 (a matched set) rather than the default 个 — 一套房子 is literally "one set of house," the same 套 used for a suit of clothes or a full set of dishes, treating a house as a complete bundle of rooms rather than a single countable item.

examples.pinyin: Zhège fángzi yòu dà yòu gānjìng.
examples.english: This house is big and clean.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng zū yí ge xiǎo fángzi.
examples.english: I want to rent a small house.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — marks actions done by hand, as in 打, 推, 拿; 拉 is to pull.
立 (lì) hints at the sound: 拉 lā is close, as in 垃 lā.

example.pinyin: Tā lāzhe wǒ de shǒu.
example.english: He is pulling me by the hand.
example.fact: 拉 is the opposite of 推 (tuī, to push), and the sign on a door says 拉 for 'pull'. It extends to 拉琴 (play a bowed instrument), 拉肚子 (to have diarrhea) and 拉近 (to bring closer), so context matters.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng lā yíxià zhè shàn mén.
examples.english: Please pull this door.

examples.pinyin: Tā huì lā xiǎotíqín.
examples.english: She can play the violin.

components.note: 衣 (clothes) — a picture of a coat with a collar and sleeves. As a radical it is 衤 on the left: 裤 trousers, 衬 shirt, 被 quilt.
月 (moon / flesh) — on the left, likely a squashed 舟 (boat) in 服, not a moon or body part. Dictionary story: a person 卩 putting on a coat 月.
卩 (kneeling person) — on the right, with 又 (hand). The old picture is a hand pressing someone down, 'submit'; clothes (衣服) and service (服务) came later.

example.hanzi: 这件衣服是我妈妈买的。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu shì wǒ māma mǎi de.
example.english: These clothes were bought by my mom.
example.fact: 衣 by itself is a pictograph of a robe's crossed collar and folded sides, and originally named an upper garment specifically — 衣服 broadened over time into a catch-all word for clothing in general, no matter which part of the body it covers.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ de yīfu zhēn hǎokàn.
examples.english: Your clothes look really nice.

examples.pinyin: Tiān lěng le, duō chuān diǎn yīfu.
examples.english: It's getting cold, wear more clothes.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — sound and speech, as in 吃, 唱, 问.
斤 (jīn, axe) is only a loose clue for tīng; the traditional 聽 had 耳 ear.
讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 请, 谢, 话.
兑 (duì) is a loose sound clue for shuō; 兑 also sounds out 脱 tuō, 税 shuì and 悦 yuè.

example.hanzi: 我听说他要搬到北京去了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ tīngshuō tā yào bān dào Běijīng qù le.
example.english: I heard he's moving to Beijing.
example.fact: 听说 reports something secondhand without vouching for it, and always opens the sentence (听说 + clause) — it never takes a direct object the way English "hear" can ("I heard the news" needs 听到 or 听见 instead, not 听说).

examples.pinyin: Tīngshuō zhè jiā diàn hěn hǎochī.
examples.english: I heard this restaurant is delicious.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ méi tīngshuōguo zhè jiàn shì.
examples.english: I've never heard of this.

components.note: 攵 (tap, hand with stick) — actions taken on something: 教, 放, 改; 救 is to take action to rescue.
求 (qiú) is a near sound match for jiù; 求 also means ask for help.

example.pinyin: Qǐng jiùjiu wǒ!
example.english: Please save me!
example.fact: 救 is the standard verb for rescuing from danger: 救命 ('help!', literally 'save life'), 急救 (first aid) and 救护车 (ambulance). It is stronger than 帮 (bāng, to help) and implies someone was in real trouble.

examples.hanzi: 有人掉进水里，快去救他！
examples.pinyin: Yǒu rén diàojìn shuǐ lǐ, kuài qù jiù tā!
examples.english: Someone fell into the water, go save him!

examples.pinyin: Yīshēng jiùle hěn duō rén de mìng.
examples.english: The doctor saved many lives.

components.note: 参 (cān) is a sound clue for 惨 cǎn and 掺 chān; the old shape pictured three stars.
力 (strength) — with 口 mouth: adding strength by words, hence to add, to increase. 加 also in 架 jià and 驾 jià.

example.hanzi: 我们都参加了昨天的会议。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dōu cānjiā le zuótiān de huìyì.
example.english: We all attended the meeting yesterday.
example.fact: 参加 pairs with events you take part in (参加会议 "attend a meeting", 参加比赛 "enter a competition") — for joining an organization as an ongoing member, Chinese instead reaches for 加入, a common point of confusion since English "join" covers both.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng cānjiā zhè cì bǐsài ma?
examples.english: Do you want to take part in this competition?

examples.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu cānjiā wǒ de hūnlǐ.
examples.english: He didn't attend my wedding.

components.note: 力 (strength) — effort, as in 助, 男, 努: handling things takes effort. The two dots stand in for 辡 of the traditional 辦.
氵 (water) — water, as in 河, 海, 清: in the old form 灋, water stood for fairness, so law and method.

example.hanzi: 我们得想个办法解决这个问题。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen děi xiǎng gè bànfǎ jiějué zhège wèntí.
example.english: We have to think of a way to solve this problem.
example.fact: 办法 almost always follows a "think of" verb — 想办法 ("think of a way") and 没办法 ("nothing can be done") are two of Mandarin's most common fixed phrases built on this word, the second doubling as a stock exclamation of resignation.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ yǒu shénme hǎo bànfǎ ma?
examples.english: Do you have any good ideas?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shízài méi bànfǎ le.
examples.english: I really have no way out.

components.note: 目 (eye) — eyes and seeing: 看 look, 眼 eye, 睛 eyeball; sleep is when the eyes close.
垂 (chuí, droop) hints at the sound and the image: drooping eyelids. Also in 锤 chuí.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng zǎodiǎnr shuì.
example.english: I want to go to bed earlier.
example.fact: 睡 usually appears in 睡觉 (to sleep), where 觉 is a separate noun, so the verb can be split as 睡了一觉 ('slept a sleep'). It can also be a result complement: 睡着 (to fall asleep) and 睡醒 (to wake up).

examples.pinyin: Bǎobao yǐjīng shuìzháo le.
examples.english: The baby has fallen asleep.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuówǎn shuì de hǎo ma?
examples.english: Did you sleep well last night?

components.note: 口 (mouth) — speech and sound, as in 吃, 唱, 问: 唯 first meant a quick reply, yes.
隹 (zhuī, short-tailed bird) is a close sound clue for wéi; 隹 also in 维 wéi and 惟 wéi.
一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ wéiyī de péngyou.
example.english: She is my only friend.
example.fact: 唯 alone already means "only, alone" as a formal, literary word, and 一 means "one" — 唯一 doubles up "only" and "one" into a single emphatic word that sits directly before a noun, the way an adjective would.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ wéiyī de jīhuì.
examples.english: This is my only chance.

examples.hanzi: 他是唯一会说法语的人。
examples.pinyin: Tā shì wéiyī huì shuō Fǎyǔ de rén.
examples.english: He's the only one who speaks French.

components.note: 回 (return) — a swirl or whirlpool drawn as nested squares: it turns around and comes back.
土 (earth) — the top part, the ground family as in 地, 场, 块. Memory aid: leave the ground 土 and go off on your own 厶 path.
厶 (private, small loop) — the bottom part. Old forms show a person leaving a place, so the 土 story is only a mnemonic.

example.pinyin: Tiān hēi le, wǒmen gāi huíqu le.
example.english: It's getting dark, we should head back.
example.fact: 回去 pairs 回 ("to return") with the directional complement 去 ("away from the speaker") — swapping in 来 gives 回来 ("to come back, toward the speaker"), the same 来/去 vantage-point contrast that also splits 进来/进去 and 下来/下去 elsewhere in this batch.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ shénme shíhou huíqu?
examples.english: When are you going back?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng huíqu kànkan bà mā.
examples.english: I want to go back and see my parents.

components.note: 人 (person) — a side-view figure of a person walking. As a radical it appears as 亻 on the left: 你 他 们.
亻 (person) — marks words about people, as in 你 you, 他 he, 做 do. Here it shows 们 pluralises person words (我们, 他们).
门 (mén) gives the sound: 们 is men (neutral tone), the same syllable as 门 gate.

example.hanzi: 人们都喜欢在公园里散步。
example.pinyin: Rénmen dōu xǐhuan zài gōngyuán lǐ sànbù.
example.english: People like taking walks in the park.
example.fact: 人们 refers to people in general as a collective, almost always as the subject of a broad statement about society — it sounds odd for a small, specific group you can point to, where Chinese would just say 这些人 ("these people") instead.

examples.hanzi: 城市里的人们生活很忙。
examples.pinyin: Chéngshì lǐ de rénmen shēnghuó hěn máng.
examples.english: People in the city lead busy lives.

examples.hanzi: 人们常常用手机买东西。
examples.pinyin: Rénmen chángcháng yòng shǒujī mǎi dōngxi.
examples.english: People often shop with their phones.

components.note: 日 (sun) — time and day, as in 早 early, 时 time, 明 bright; 晚 is when the sun is late.
免 (miǎn) is a close sound clue for wǎn; it also sounds out 勉 miǎn and 挽 wǎn.

example.pinyin: Jīnwǎn nǐ yǒu kòng ma?
example.english: Are you free tonight?
example.fact: 晚 means 'late' as an adjective (来晚了, 'arrived late') and 'evening' as a noun, as in 晚上 and 晚饭 (dinner). Greetings use it too: 晚安 ('good night') and 晚上好 ('good evening') are common.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zěnme zhème wǎn cái huílái?
examples.english: Why are you coming back so late?

examples.pinyin: Wǎnfàn nǐ xiǎng chī shénme?
examples.english: What do you want for dinner?

components.note: 讠 (speech) — words, as in 说, 请, 谢: 该 is what one ought to say or do.
亥 (hài) is a close sound clue for gāi; 亥 also sounds out 孩 hái, 核 hé and 刻 kè.
歹 (bad bone) — death and decay, as in 残 remnant, 烈 fierce, 殊 special.
匕 (person) — a person beside bones: death.

example.pinyin: “Gāisǐ! Wǒ bǎ yàoshi wàng zài jiā lǐ le.”
example.english: "Damn it! I left my keys at home."
example.fact: 该死 literally means "ought to die" (该 "should" + 死 "to die") — much like the English curse "damn it" (literally invoking damnation), its original violence has faded through overuse into a mild exclamation of frustration, not a real wish for anyone's death.

examples.hanzi: 该死,我又错过了公交车!
examples.pinyin: Gāisǐ, wǒ yòu cuòguòle gōngjiāochē!
examples.english: Damn, I missed the bus again!

examples.hanzi: 这该死的天气,又下雨了。
examples.pinyin: Zhè gāisǐ de tiānqì, yòu xiàyǔ le.
examples.english: This damned weather, it's raining again.

components.note: 门 (gate, door) — 门 is a gate, as in 开, 关, 问, 间; 闭 puts a bar across it, so shut.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bìshang yǎnjing.
example.english: Please close your eyes.
example.fact: 闭 is more literary than 关 (guān): you 关门 (close a door) but 闭眼 or 闭嘴 (shut one's mouth) for body parts. It also appears in 闭幕 (close a ceremony) and 开闭 (open and close).

examples.pinyin: Tā lèi de bìshàngle yǎnjing.
examples.english: He was so tired that he closed his eyes.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng bìshàng zuǐ, ānjìng yíxià.
examples.english: Please close your mouth and be quiet for a moment.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 过, 近, 进: to go and pick.
先 (xiān) is a close sound clue for xuǎn; 先 also in 洗 xǐ.
扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 打, 拿, 抱: picking out with the hand.
圣 stands in for 睪 of 擇, a loose sound clue for zé; the original shows up in 泽 zé.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen yǒu hěn duō xuǎnzé.
example.english: We have many choices.
example.fact: 选择 works as both a verb ("to choose") and a noun ("a choice") with no change in form — 做选择 ("to make a choice") uses it as the object of 做, while 选择 placed before another noun or verb acts as the verb itself.

examples.hanzi: 你可以选择自己喜欢的颜色。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ xuǎnzé zìjǐ xǐhuan de yánsè.
examples.english: You can choose the color you like.

examples.pinyin: Tā xuǎnzéle liú zài jiāxiāng.
examples.english: He chose to stay in his hometown.

components.note: 土 (earth) — soil and land: 地, 场, 块; 坏 first meant to collapse, as of a wall of earth.
不 (bù) is only a stand-in for the old sound part 褱 (huái); a loose clue for huài.

example.pinyin: Zhège shǒujī huài le.
example.english: This phone is broken.
example.fact: 坏 means 'bad' for people and things, 'broken' for objects (坏了) and 'spoiled' for food. It is also used as a result complement to show something has been ruined: 玩坏 (broke through playing), 吃坏肚子 (to get a stomach ache from food).

examples.pinyin: Zhège píngguǒ huài le, bié chī.
examples.english: This apple has gone bad, don't eat it.

examples.pinyin: Jīntiān tiānqì huài tòu le.
examples.english: The weather is terrible today.

components.note: 厂 (cliff) — cliffs and rocks, as in 厅 hall, 厚 thick: a spring flowing from a cliff.
泉 (spring) — water from the rock: the source (源 yuán adds 氵 later); 原 is source, origin.
囗 (enclosure) — here a mat; oldest form shows a person 大 lying on a mat, "to rely on", later "cause". 因 also sounds out 姻 yīn and 烟 yān.

example.hanzi: 他没有说明迟到的原因。
example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu shuōmíng chídào de yuányīn.
example.english: He didn't explain the reason for being late.
example.fact: 原因 names the cause behind something and pairs naturally with 说明 ("to explain") or 找 ("to look for") — its counterpart 结果 ("result", also in this batch) often appears right alongside it in the fixed phrase 原因和结果, "cause and effect."

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zhīdào shìqing de yuányīn ma?
examples.english: Do you know the reason for it?

examples.pinyin: Yuányīn hěn jiǎndān, wǒ tài lèi le.
examples.english: The reason is simple: I was too tired.

components.note: 下 (below) — a mark placed under a line, the mirror of 上 above.
土 (earth) — the top part, the ground family as in 地, 场, 块. Memory aid: leave the ground 土 and go off on your own 厶 path.
厶 (private, small loop) — the bottom part. Old forms show a person leaving a place, so the 土 story is only a mnemonic.

example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí shuō xiàqù, méiyǒu tíng.
example.english: He kept talking on and on, without stopping.
example.fact: Beyond its literal "to go down" (走下去 "to walk down"), 下去 attached after almost any verb extends an action into the future — 说下去 ("keep talking"), 坚持下去 ("keep persisting") — an abstract extension mirroring what 起来 (pilot batch) does for actions just beginning, rather than continuing.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen zǒu xiàqu kànkan ba.
examples.english: Let's walk down and have a look.

examples.pinyin: Zhèyàng xiàqu bù xíng.
examples.english: We can't go on like this.

components.note: 又 (hand) — two hands pass a vessel: one gives, one receives; 授 shòu adds 扌 for "give".

example.pinyin: Tā shòu le hěn duō kǔ.
example.english: He suffered a lot.
example.fact: 受 often appears in set phrases: 受伤 (to be hurt), 受欢迎 (to be popular), 受不了 (cannot stand). It can be used both for receiving good things (受到表扬, 'receive praise') and for suffering bad ones.

examples.pinyin: Tā zài lùshang shòule shāng.
examples.english: He got hurt on the road.

examples.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng hěn shòu huānyíng.
examples.english: This movie is very popular.

components.note: 辶 (movement) — marks walking and roads, as in 过, 进, 送; 连 is vehicles 车 moving in a line, joined together.
车 (cart) — the vehicle in the chain, as in 转, 轮; 链 liàn (chain) is built on 连.

example.pinyin: Tā lián fàn dōu méi chī.
example.english: He didn't even eat.
example.fact: The 连…都/也 pattern means 'even…': 连我都知道 ('even I know'). 连 also means 'to connect' (连接) and 'continuously' (连续), and it appears in names of cities and chains such as 连锁 (chain store).

examples.pinyin: Zhème jiǎndān, lián xiǎohái dōu huì.
examples.english: It's so simple that even a child can do it.

examples.pinyin: Zhè liǎng ge fángjiān shì liánzhe de.
examples.english: These two rooms are connected.

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈, 她, 姐.
子 (child) — a woman with her child: the picture of something good.
女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈, 她, 姐.
子 (child) — a woman with her child: the picture of something good.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào hǎohǎo zhàogù zìjǐ.
example.english: You need to take good care of yourself.
example.fact: 好好 reduplicates the adjective 好 ("good") into an adverb meaning "properly, thoroughly" right before a verb — colloquially it's often extended with the diminutive suffix 儿 (好好儿) and a shifted spoken tone on the second syllable, a common spoken variant that written pinyin references don't always show.

examples.pinyin: Hǎohǎo xuéxí, tiāntiān xiàngshàng.
examples.english: Study hard and improve every day.

examples.hanzi: 他好好的,怎么突然生病了?
examples.pinyin: Tā hǎohāo de, zěnme tūrán shēngbìng le?
examples.english: He was perfectly fine; how did he suddenly get sick?

components.note: 玉 (jade) — jade put away safely: 全 first meant flawless, pure, then whole.

example.pinyin: Quán jiā rén dōu zài kàn diànshì.
example.english: The whole family is watching TV.
example.fact: 全 can be an adjective ('whole', 全世界), an adverb ('completely', 全懂了) and a verb-like word ('complete', 齐全). A classic grammar point is that 全 modifies the noun directly, whereas 都 comes before the verb.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen quán jiā dōu xǐhuan lǚxíng.
examples.english: Our whole family loves traveling.

examples.pinyin: Zhèxiē tí wǒ quán zuòduì le.
examples.english: I got all these questions right.

components.note: 石 (stone) — stone and hardness, as in 碎 shatter, 破 break, 码 code: 确 is solid, certain.
角 (jiǎo) replaces 隺 (hè) of 確 and is only a loose clue for què.
宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 家, 字, 室: a house stocked with goods, so solid and real.

example.pinyin: Tā quèshí hěn nǔlì.
example.english: He really is very hardworking.
example.fact: 确实 confirms that something is true or accurate, often responding to doubt — unlike 真的, its more casual spoken counterpart, 确实 leans formal and shows up more often in writing, news, and considered speech.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì quèshí hěn qíguài.
examples.english: This matter is indeed strange.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ quèshí xūyào xiūxi le.
examples.english: You really do need a rest.

components.note: 扌 (hand, 提手旁) — marks hand actions, as in 拉 pull, 推 push; 挺 is straightening up and sticking out, then very, as in 挺好.
廷 (tíng) — same sound: 挺 tǐng. 廷 also sounds out 庭 tíng and 艇 tǐng.

example.pinyin: Jīntiān tǐng lěng de.
example.english: It's quite cold today.
example.fact: As an adverb, 挺 means 'quite' or 'pretty' and is colloquial and mild, often followed by 的: 挺好的 ('pretty good'). As a verb it means 'to straighten up' or 'to endure', as in 挺住 ('hold on!').

examples.pinyin: Zhège diànyǐng tǐng hǎokàn de.
examples.english: This movie is quite good.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ juéde tā tǐng búcuò de.
examples.english: I think he's pretty nice.

components.note: 此 (cǐ) is a sound clue for 紫 zǐ, 雌 cí and 些 xiē; as a word it means "this".

example.pinyin: Cǐ rén shì wǒ de péngyou.
example.english: This person is my friend.
example.fact: 此 is the formal or written counterpart of 这, found in set phrases like 因此 (therefore), 此外 (besides), 如此 (like this) and 此时 (at this moment). It is rarely used alone in speech.

examples.pinyin: Cǐ shí cǐ kè, wǒ hěn kāixīn.
examples.english: Right at this moment, I'm happy.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng liúyì cǐ shì, búyào wàngjì.
examples.english: Please keep this matter in mind and don't forget it.

components.note: 水 (water) — a picture of flowing water; as a radical it appears as 氵 on the left (海, 河) or 水 at the bottom (泉, 冰).

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē shuǐ.
example.english: I want to drink water.
example.fact: 水 is one of the oldest radicals, written as 氵 on the left of characters for liquids and rivers. It also appears in everyday words like 水果 (fruit), 水平 (level, standard) and in the common saying 一水之隔 ('separated by a river').

examples.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi lěngshuǐ.
examples.english: Please give me a glass of cold water.

examples.pinyin: Hé lǐ de shuǐ hěn gānjìng.
examples.english: The water in the river is very clean.

components.note: 氵 (water) — water and mixing liquids, as in 河, 海, 清: 混 is to mix or muddy.
昆 (kūn) is a close sound clue for hùn; 昆 also in 棍 gùn.
虫 (insect, creature) — small animals and insects, as in 蚊 mosquito, 蛇 snake, 虾 shrimp: 蛋 is the egg of a creature.

example.pinyin: “Nǐ zhège húndàn!” tā shēngqì de shuō.
example.english: "You bastard!" she said angrily.
example.fact: 混 is read here with its colloquial second tone hún ("muddled, foolish") rather than its more common fourth-tone reading hùn ("to mix"). 蛋 ("egg") is one of Mandarin's most productive insult suffixes, also seen in 坏蛋 ("bad egg, scoundrel") and 笨蛋 ("fool," literally "stupid egg").

examples.hanzi: 别骂人,说混蛋是不礼貌的。
examples.pinyin: Bié màrén, shuō húndàn shì bù lǐmào de.
examples.english: Don't swear; saying "scoundrel" is impolite.

examples.hanzi: 他骂了那个人一声混蛋。
examples.pinyin: Tā màle nàge rén yì shēng húndàn.
examples.english: He called that person a scoundrel.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 木 is wood — cups were first made of wood, as in 桌, 板, 树.
不 (bù) — loose hint — 杯 is bēi; 不 shares just the b- start.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi chá.
example.english: Please give me a cup of tea.
example.fact: 杯 works as both a noun (杯子, a cup) and a measure word for drinks: 一杯水, 两杯咖啡. It also appears in 干杯 ('cheers', literally 'dry the cup'), which is said before drinking together at a meal.

examples.pinyin: Zhuōzi shang yǒu liǎng bēi kāfēi.
examples.english: There are two cups of coffee on the table.

examples.pinyin: Zhège bēizi shì wǒ de.
examples.english: This cup is mine.

components.note: 亻 (person) — people, as in 你, 他, 们: 保 oldest form shows a person carrying a child on the back, so to protect.
呆 here is the old child shape 子 beside the person, a picture of keeping safe.
讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 谢: to prove by saying.
正 (zhèng) gives the exact sound; 正 also in 整 zhěng and 政 zhèng.

example.hanzi: 我向你保证,这件事不会再发生。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xiàng nǐ bǎozhèng, zhè jiàn shì bú huì zài fāshēng.
example.english: I guarantee you, this won't happen again.
example.fact: 保证 introduces a promise and is almost always followed directly by the content of that promise as a full clause — "我向你保证..." ("I guarantee/promise you that...") is a fixed, formal way to open a solemn assurance.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bǎozhèng zhǔnshí dào.
examples.english: I promise to arrive on time.

examples.hanzi: 这个产品有一年的保证。
examples.pinyin: Zhège chǎnpǐn yǒu yì nián de bǎozhèng.
examples.english: This product has a one-year guarantee.

components.note: 子 (child) — a child learning under a roof: the top shows hands over a house, and the child 子 below. Also gives 觉 jué its upper part.
木 (tree) — wood and trees, as in 树, 林, 桌: 校 first meant a wooden frame or restraint.
交 (jiāo) is a close sound clue for xiào; 交 also in 较 jiào and 校 xiào.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǒulù qù xuéxiào.
example.english: I walk to school every day.
example.fact: 学 pictures children (子) gathered under a roof (冖) to study, and 校 originally meant a wooden framework or enclosure before narrowing to "a place of structured learning" — 学校 combines "studying" with "an enclosed place" into a fairly transparent image of the institution itself.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de xuéxiào lí jiā hěn jìn.
examples.english: My school is close to home.

examples.hanzi: 放学后,我们在学校门口见。
examples.pinyin: Fàngxué hòu, wǒmen zài xuéxiào ménkǒu jiàn.
examples.english: After school, let's meet at the school gate.

components.note: 买 (mǎi, buy) — its sound is almost the same as 卖 mài, and the meaning is the opposite: buy and sell.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn mài shuǐguǒ.
example.english: This shop sells fruit.
example.fact: 卖 is the counterpart of 买 (mǎi, to buy) and differs only by the tone and the extra stroke on top. A famous tone pair is 买 mǎi vs. 卖 mài. It extends to 卖力 (to work hard) and 出卖 (to betray).

examples.hanzi: 这家超市卖新鲜的蔬菜。
examples.pinyin: Zhè jiā chāoshì mài xīnxiān de shūcài.
examples.english: This supermarket sells fresh vegetables.

examples.pinyin: Tā xiǎng bǎ jiù chē màidiào.
examples.english: He wants to sell his old car.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a person and his word: 言 (speech) beside it gives a person who keeps his word, hence "trust, believe".
言 (speech) — written 讠 on the left of other characters, as in 说, 请, 谢.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gěi māma xiěle yì fēng xìn.
example.english: I wrote a letter to my mother.
example.fact: 信 has two common uses: 'letter' (measure word 封) and 'to believe', as in 我不信 ('I don't believe it'). It also forms 信息 (information), 短信 (text message) and 自信 (self-confidence).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bù xiāngxìn tā shuō de huà.
examples.english: I don't believe what he said.

examples.hanzi: 我收到了一封朋友的信。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ shōudàole yì fēng péngyou de xìn.
examples.english: I received a letter from a friend.

meanings: to accept (a suggestion, punishment, bribe etc)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 打, 拿, 抱: receiving something by hand.
妾 (qiè) is only a loose sound clue for jiē.
又 (hand) — two hands pass a vessel: one gives, one receives; 授 shòu adds 扌 for "give".

example.pinyin: Tā hěn nán jiēshòu zhège shìshí.
example.english: He finds it hard to accept this fact.
example.fact: 接受 means to accept something once offered — an apology, a gift, an idea — while 接 alone just means "to receive" without any sense of agreement; adding 受 ("to bear, to undergo") is what pushes the word from mere receiving into willingly taking something on.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yuànyì jiēshòu nǐ de bāngzhù.
examples.english: I'm willing to accept your help.

examples.pinyin: Tā jiēshòule zhè fèn gōngzuò.
examples.english: He accepted this job.

components.note: 攵 (tap, strike) — hand holding a stick, as in 教 teach, 收 collect, 放 release: correcting by hand.
己 (jǐ) is a close sound clue for gǎi.
又 (hand) — the bottom, standing in for the 攴 (tap) of traditional 變. 亦 on top replaces the tangled-thread part and has no meaning link.
變 (traditional) — tangled threads and a tapping hand 攴: sorting out a mess, so 'change'. Read as 'usually explained'.

example.hanzi: 这件事改变了我的想法。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì gǎibiàn le wǒ de xiǎngfǎ.
example.english: This changed the way I think about it.
example.fact: 改变 describes a shift into a genuinely different state (改变想法 "change one's mind", 改变计划 "change plans") — for a smaller correction, like fixing a typo, Chinese instead reaches for the narrower root character 改 that 改变 itself is built from.

examples.pinyin: Tā de fàxíng gǎibiàn le.
examples.english: His hairstyle has changed.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bú yào gǎibiàn zhǔyi.
examples.english: Don't change your mind.
